utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This hearing is to take evidence from Zagreb by means of a video conference link, there being three witnesses, is that right, Mr. Sayers, for whom we have summaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In order, as we've notified the Prosecution a few weeks ago: Ivica Kristo, followed by Srecko Kristo, and finishing up with Ilija Zuljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let us see if the link is established. Can you hear us? Let the witness take the oath. COURT TECHNICIAN: The witness is being picked up at the moment. He should arrive in a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, it may be more comfortable if counsel sits down for this proceeding, particularly while we're waiting for things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kristo.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, just to introduce myself, my name is Stephen Sayers, and along with my colleague, Mr. Mitko Naumovski, we represent Dario Kordic. I would just like to ask you a few questions today, and take your time in answering, please. It's important to get a clear transcript. Could we start, please, with asking you your full name, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Ivica Kristo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, I'm going to take you very quickly through a few preliminary details regarding your personal background. It's true that you were born on April 15th, 1956, in the city of Zenica, I believe.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're married and you have two sons.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you were trained as a painter in vocational school, following which you worked for a construction firm in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before the fighting broke out, sir, in 1993, I believe that you used to live with your family in a suburb to the south-west of the city of Zenica called Raspotocje.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And during the war your wife and sons left Zenica, but you stayed there throughout the conflict.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you participated in the formation of the Zenica branch of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the formation of the Croat Defence Council formations in that city.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In October of 1992 you were appointed to serve as a reserve company commander in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Raspotocje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And following the end of the war, you left the city of Zenica and you currently live in the north of the Republic of Croatia, in the town of Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Varazdin, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And with the Court's permission, I do intend to lead the witness through most of the outline, with the exception of paragraphs 14 through 17, unless the Prosecution objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you have described in the outline that you signed on July 9th how tensions in the city of Zenica started to grow towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The first serious incident involving actions taken against the Croats was in the autumn of 1992, when the Muslims physically took over Zenica military barracks after the Serbs had left and proceeded to aim three tanks at Croat suburbs, an action which you yourself visually observed through binoculars.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the end of 1992/early 1993, Mr. Kristo, we have already heard that numerous Muslim armed formations from all over Bosnia, in addition to the local Territorial Defence, were stationed in the town. Could you just give us, please, a listing, as far as you can recall, of the Muslim armed forces that were to be found in Zenica at the end of 1992 and during 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The names?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No. MOS, Muslim forces, Mujahedin, the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Was MOS another name for the 7th Muslim Brigade, or was the 7th Muslim Brigade a detachment that was separate from MOS?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The Mujahedin were the leaders of MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But the question I asked was: Was the MOS, M-O-S, the same as the 7th Muslim Brigade, or were these two separate military units?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I take it, sir, that the large concentration of armed forces on the Muslim side in Zenica was a factor that contributed to the escalation of tension in that city between the Croat and the Muslim communities.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, in contrast to the well-armed Muslim military units in the city, sir, how well armed were the HVO military units? Could you please let us know, help us out with that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, pretty poorly. In that part where I was, in Raspotocje, less than 40 per cent of soldiers were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Proceeding, Mr. President, to paragraph 11 of the outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that there were approximately 500 or so so-called Mujahedin in the city of Zenica and that these men were both locals and from foreign countries.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit about the Mujahedin, what they did in the city, how they contributed to the escalation of tensions that you've described? Help us out with that, please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: They were quartered at Bilimisce, in the school, in the music school in the heart of Zenica, and they had vans without -- and three of them sat in front with their rifles pointing in front, because there were no windshields, and they drove around with and without permission. And they had their rifles, they had machetes, and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've also described a number of incidents involving the playing of music and the use of loudspeakers on these vehicles. Could you tell us a little bit about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you that they were airing this Arab music, which I couldn't understand, and none of us could. And this was also aired in the barracks and all the places where they were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In your outline, Mr. Kristo, you've also described the commission of acts of aggression against the population of Croat villages in the Zenica area. And you've outlined incidents such as shooting at barrels of brandy, the killing of pigs and the threatening of civilian population. Could you tell us a little bit about that? Did you see that yourself, or are you just reporting what you were told by others?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I personally experienced when they came to my uncle's house and asked him if he had any pigs. He did not. Then they came, saw the barrels and fired at them. And I saw it with -- I saw it with my own eyes when they left, and they killed two pigs belonging to a close relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And just for the Court's information, in our video exhibits at Tab 13, there's more videotape footage of this kind of activity, there's no point in showing that and wasting time. The Court can view that for itself and reach its own conclusions. Let me turn to the period just before the fighting broke out in Zenica in April of 1993, Mr. Kristo. We've already heard evidence from others that the increasing tension and the escalation of incidents between the two communities led to about 2.000 Croat civilians leaving Zenica before April of 1993; is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, did these people leave voluntarily as a result of propaganda or did they leave out of fear?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, Mr. Kristo, did you ever hear about or see anybody in Zenica trying to do anything to reduce the incidents of Mujahedin activities around the villages in your area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that you personally watched a parade in 1993, early on in 1993, where President Izetbegovic came to Zenica and reviewed Mujahedin and handed them green and black flags?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kristo, I'm just going to go forward in time to April 18th, 1993. Could you describe for the Court, please, in your own words, who attacked whom in Zenica. Which side attacked which side, please, and could you describe what life was like during the first few days of that attack, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Between the 18th and 19th, that is, at 5.15 in the morning, our headquarters at Podbrijezje was attacked and they also immediately set out to conquer where we had our guards and everything because they had prepared it all against all the hill features where -- which we held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You just said that at 5.15 in the morning your headquarters in Podbrijezje was attacked. Attacked by whom?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Together the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the so-called one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Some suggestion has been made in the course of this case, Mr. Kristo, that it was actually the HVO that supposedly attacked ABiH forces in Zenica. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I have to say that that is not true because I was there throughout the war, and all the rest, and I know because I saw them come out of the barracks, the direction they were going and what places they were taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 17 of your outline, you describe the fact that you were hugely outnumbered. In your estimation, Mr. Kristo, what was the ratio between the number of attacking ABiH forces and the number of defending HVO forces? Can you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: One to ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Ten ABiH troops for every HVO soldier; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir, and you have described that the HVO surrendered to the TO military police on April 19th, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So in total, there would have been about one, or at most two days of actual combat between the attacking ABiH forces and the defending HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: It started in the morning and by the afternoon, it was all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, were any representations made to you about what would happen to you if you elected to surrender to the TO military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that we would suffer no consequences if we surrendered our weapons and that they would protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: After we surrendered the weapons in Raspotocje, about which I'm talking Mujahedin also arrived and the TO, the Territorial Defence police ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I understand the position to be that they are working on the connection. We'll wait for a few minutes and see if it can be re-established. If it can, of course we'll go on in the usual way. If not, we'll take a break. The news is that the lines are down in Zagreb, or to Zagreb. The result being, obviously, that we can't go on for the moment. What we'll do is we'll take the adjournment now for a quarter of an hour in any event, and if lines are not reconnected, of course, it will have to be longer. --- Break taken at 10.07 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I understand the line has been re-established. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, before we had that unscheduled break, you were discussing the assurances made to you by the Mujahedin that you would not be imprisoned, and then you were describing what actually happened. What did actually happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you, Mr. Kristo, unfortunately there's a technical problem here in that we're not getting an English translations of what you're saying. The English translation is coming over the Croatian channel, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can it be heard now? Is it coming now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry about this, Mr. Kristo, but perhaps I could just ask you to describe when you were imprisoned, for how long, please, and the conditions under which you were detained in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Three days. Three or four days later they came and called me to what they called an information interview at KPD prison. The ABiH military police took me there, not to the main entrance but to the side entrance, and they held me there for four days. They released me on the fifth day. Meanwhile they abused me. They were asking about the rest of the weapons, the mortars and other things, where had we hidden it. And that was not true, because we had surrendered everything. I was mistreated at the KPD. I was tied to a radiator. I was constantly abused, with very little food. I had almost nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you say that you were constantly abused, Mr. Kristo, was that verbal abuse or physical abuse, or both?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I think that you've just described that you were taken to the KPD prison premises. Is it also right that other Croat prisoners were taken to the Babina elementary school by Mujahedin and also to the music school facility in Bilimisce that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you were detained a second time on the 16th of October, 1993, Mr. Kristo. Could you just describe the length of that detention and what happened to you during the time that you were detained.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I was arrested again on 16 October, in front of my house. They surrounded me. They came in a white Golf and they again said, with their weapons pointed at me, that I was being taken to an information interview, and I was taken to Bilimisce. I know I was there until the afternoon. Then they put me in a van, the same one I had described before that belonged to MOS. And then they took me -- they took a left turn and took me through the city, but I couldn't orient myself anymore. Then they brought me to that location which I could not recognise, and later on I learned that that was the Babina elementary school. Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who were your captors?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: There were two Mujahedin, two Arabs, and two MOS members, Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And how long were you detained, sir, at this facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I spent 40 days at the Babina elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you describe what happened to you during that 40-day detention by the Mujahedin and MOS members.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Every night I was in a room with two persons I had not known. One said that he was from Kakanj and the other one from Breza. And every night I could hear, from 2.00 a.m. until 4.35 in the morning, I could hear screams in other rooms. Also the three of us were taken out individually every second, every third sometimes, every fifth day, and abused. They beat us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were these beatings simply with fists or with implements too?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Fists and rubber batons. It was also the rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I take it that you were physically injured fairly badly as a result of these regular beatings that were administered to you.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Also we suffered from the lack of food in those 40 days. I can say that I ate, all in all, about one kilogram of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you lose any body weight during the detention that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English Transcripts. endured, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. When I was arrested, I weighed about 100 kilos, and after I was released, 40 days later, I weighed 72 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just wind up the questions that I have for you, Mr. Kristo, and thank you very much for your patience. You've described in your outline being a witness to several shells, artillery shells falling on Zenica on April 19th, 1993. Just a couple of questions in connection with this subject, sir. First, had Zenica been shelled by the Bosnian Serb army artillery before this date, before April 19th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you made some conclusions or you've given some conclusions in paragraph 23 of your outline regarding where these shells came from, in your estimation. Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The shells came from the positions on Mount Vlasic, where the Serbs were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Serb artillery deployed on Mount Vlasic had sufficient range to reach the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know -- I take it that you're saying that in your estimation, the BSA artillery did have the range to reach Zenica from positions on Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, thank you very much. No further questions at this time, from me, anyway. And now I believe that Mr. Cerkez's lawyer, Goran Mikulicic, may have some questions for you, but maybe he does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kristo. My name is Goran Mikulicic, I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and in this matter I represent Mr. Cerkez's interests. I have only several questions for you, and will you please answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Kristo, you told us that you were personally present in early 1993 in Zenica, when President Izetbegovic, Alija Izetbegovic, personally reviewed the troops there.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, do you recall how Mr. Izetbegovic, as President of the BH republic, saluted the ABiH troops?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: "Allah-u-ekber".

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It was not coming-- there it is in the record. It was in Arabic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: He said, "Selam Aleikum" and they responded, "Allah-u-ekber".

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that unusual for you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also told us that President Izetbegovic handed them over the green and black flag.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And this was shown on Zenica television. Was this flag an official flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What type of flag was it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The official BiH flag was the one with lilies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the other one?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't know about those two flags. I don't know what the green one or the black one represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kristo, you described your suffering in Zenica --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- and suffering of other Croats there. If someone was to tell you that the mistreatment of Croats in Zenica at that time were part of disinformation, would that be correct or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: That would be disinformation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, perhaps we did not understand each other. Is it correct that Croats in Zenica, and you personally, were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question to you, Mr. Kristo, while you were in prison, you said that you were brought for interviews with the police and army security officers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name Ramiz Suvalic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he come to the prison for interviews?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you heard that he had come for some others?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, those who had entered through the main entrance, he was with them. I entered through the side entrance, and I was only interviewed by the lower-ranking officials and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Kristo, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have some questions for you from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say in your summary that you were involved in the formation of the HDZ in Zenica and of the HVO. How senior or junior were you in either of those organisations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: In the HDZ, I was simply a member. In the HVO, I was commander of the reserve troops of Raspotocje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings of the leadership of either the HDZ or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't always have that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, I'll just repeat the last question because you may not have heard it, and that is --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I had not heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- did you attend any meetings of the leadership of either the HDZ or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, did you hear the question this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm told it's the thunderstorm in Zagreb and not you, but I don't know whether it would be sensible to use another microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me try. While we're waiting for the connection, what I will do is, having got an answer to the question, go straight to the absolutely critical questions I must ask in case the rest of the call is unsuccessful. It means I shan't be dealing with things strictly chronologically, but I hope that will be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you hear us, Mr. Kristo? Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, let's see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, did you hear the question I asked you sometime ago about being present at meetings of the leadership?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just answer that question?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: As far as the HDZ meetings is concerned, only large rallies and not the leadership meetings. As far as the HVO is concerned, it was just for guidance, but I did not participate in any top meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the moment I'm going to go right to the end of your evidence, for fear further breaks in transmission between here and Zagreb, so that I can deal with the matters that you dealt with last. You say that you were detained on what, the 18th or the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: It was not 18th or 19th, it was three days following the conflict which was around the 21st. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason I ask you that is because in the summary of yours that's been served on us, you say that they started arresting all Croats on the 20th, but you say that by the 19th they'd already imprisoned all military men from Cajdras?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is what I said. I was at Raspotocje, not at Cajdras.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How far is Raspotocje from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: From the town itself, three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to clarify this, you're not suggesting that there was an attack by the ABiH on Zenica itself on either the 18th or the 19th of April, are you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: 18th to 19th, the ABiH attacked the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But not actually in Zenica itself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Wherever the HVO was deployed, everything was attacked simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't in Zenica on the 18th, were you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's then my mistake for not understanding what you've told us. You were in there on the 18th, but you didn't surrender then?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: We surrendered on the 19th, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on the 19th, where were you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: At Raspotocje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you been there all day on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So were you taken into custody straight away on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No. Two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So having surrendered, what did you do? Did you stay in your barracks, or what happened? What was the form of the surrender?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The ABiH police told us that everyone was surrendered, that we should not try anything, that we should surrender peacefully, that we should turn over the weapons, and that they would guarantee our lives and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event, throughout the 19th, you were at Raspotocje and you were not in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. That is a suburb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were there for -- several kilometres away from where the shells landed when they landed near to the radio station?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: From the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You were several -- thank you. You say that there was a generalised attack on the HVO, but are you aware that on the 19th, people were in the centre of Zenica, going about their business of shopping and so on, and it was such people that were killed by the shells that landed.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the next thing is this: Are you aware, from what you will have heard at the time, that Radio Zenica was the only local radio station at that time that was not under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Radio Zenica was not under the HVO control, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's correct. And indeed its broadcasts were upsetting to and irritating to the HVO, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the military, where you were a reserve company commander, did you or did you not have any particular skill in relation to heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No. No. We only had guard duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You have no expertise in relation to artillery shells of any kind.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was in the military, in the former military, where we had exercise, and I was a crewman with a tank crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you've told us in your evidence, and indeed in your summary, that you were present and watched the shelling of Zenica, but that simply isn't right, is it; you weren't present.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I was about 500 metres away from where the shells fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand that, because you've just told me you were in the place where your barracks were all day, and that was several kilometres away. You told us that you were there all day on the 19th, so you can't have been 500 metres away. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I was at Raspotocje, and from Raspotocje, that direction, it could be about 500. From my house, one can see the whole of the former Tito Street, where the shells were falling near the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't have a plan of the area with sufficient detail to pick up Raspotocje at the moment, and we can't use overhead projectors with you in Zagreb, but did you not tell me some questions ago that Raspotocje -- was it four or five kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three kilometres away from the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. That is Raspotocje from the beginning. The whole Raspotocje to the end of Raspotocje is some five or six kilometres. That is what the beginning of Raspotocje is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you say that you were able to say where these shells came from. How were you able to do that, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, because I was looking straight towards the centre of the town and the shells were falling in my direction, that is, facing me. And when it fell on the asphalt, I saw it splinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points about that, then. First, you weren't being accurate when you told me a few questions ago that you weren't aware of people being about the town doing their ordinary business, because you must have been able to see the people in the street. Did you see the people in the street?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, I saw people, what they were doing. I mean, I saw people moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second thing is: Simply from seeing a shell land, you cannot tell the direction from which it came, can you? You can only tell the direction from which it came if you actually see the fire or light that comes when the shell is actually fired.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: You can't see the gun which fired the shell, but you can conclude where it arrived from, because I know where Zenica is and I know where Vlasic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you couldn't see the trajectory, you couldn't see the path of the shell, because the paths of shells are invisible to the naked eye because they're too fast.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but one can see the flame.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you didn't see the flame coming from Vlasic; you just simply saw, if your evidence is correct --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I know. I saw where the shell landed on the street and where the fragments then fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you looking out specially for this shell or was it by chance that you saw it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: It just happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know that the HVO had artillery on Puticevo, don't you; you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know where Puticevo is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I've heard, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that Zenica then was attacked on the 18th of April. Can you give us the details of what you say was the nature of the attack upon it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: We were attacked, and their sole objective was to capture us and to have us lay down the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake for not being clear. What actually do you say happened in Zenica? Forget what happened at your barracks. What do you say actually happened in Zenica, so far as the HVO was concerned, and when?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Nothing happened in Zenica, because everybody had left Zenica to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English Transcripts. Podbrezje. Then we were in Raspotocje, and all the units were out of Zenica. Nobody was in the town except the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So, and I think I touched on this earlier, there was, in fact, no attack within Zenica by the ABiH on the HVO on the 18th or 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Where the police was in the school --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't not hear the end of the sentence. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The police were in the school. I think the interpreters would be grateful if you'd just repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The school Sestra Ditri [phoen] is where the HVO police was. And what was going on there, I don't know, because I was at Raspotocje, but they were there and that was the only thing that was in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All other HVO had left the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, we were all out of the town Raspotocje, Gornje, Zenica, Podbrezje, along the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And no Croats would be left around in the town, or very few; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: The civilians were there, but the troops that were there, they had pulled out of Zenica, left Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to accept or challenge your account of your own imprisonment, but just help us with this: You say that you were rearrested on the 16th of October. Was anything said to you by those detaining you about what reason they had to do this to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: For interviews, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But no other explanation ever given beyond that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you ever given any earlier account in the form of a statement about your experiences to any other body, investigating judge, or anything of that sort, or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I did not, because there were threats; if anyone learned of it, then that would be the end of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that was threats at the time, presumably, you mean?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, in the school, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since then, you haven't made any statements to any other body, international or national, about your experience?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No, to no one. To no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm dealing with things out of order, but it's for the reason I gave before. Having become the company -- the reserve company commander that you were, did you go to the swearing-in ceremony in December of 1992 in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go to any such ceremonies ever?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: I was at the HDZ rally and I wasn't at the troop review.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HDZ rally, when was that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who ran that rally, who were the main speakers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, Josip Pojavnik, Mirko Sakic, he was the president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anybody else that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, that was the Zenica area. I know them, and they were among the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to take this witness through the items that I dealt with with the other witness yesterday when we can go through documents. In the circumstances, that's all I'm going to ask him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No more questions, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, thank you for giving your evidence to the Tribunal. You are released and free to go. Thank you. And we'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, can we have the picture from Zagreb, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kristo. Will you please give your name to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Good morning, I am Srecko Kristo. I was born on the 19th of June, 1954 in the village of Kaonik, municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I shall lead you through most of your statement, with the Court's leave, to try to bring this to an end as quickly as possible because we have some technical difficulties. Would you just listen to my questions and give us short answers. You are married and a father of two, and with your family you live in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are in the restaurant business and that was what you have devoted your career to. For the past 12 years, you had your own restaurant in Busovaca and that is where you work; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, on the 24th of January 1993, you went from Busovaca to Kiseljak with a friend of yours, Igor Bogdanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You set off around 9.00 in the morning, and in point of fact, you were going to Konjic because you were going to buy a jeep there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In Konjic, you did buy the jeep as you were planning to do and you returned to Kiseljak sometime around 1400 or rather slightly before that.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And after a short stop in Kiseljak, you set off to -- for Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And on your way from Kiseljak to Busovaca, you dropped into a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I shall repeat the question. On your way from Kiseljak to Busovaca, you stopped by a coffee -- a cafe called Jelenov Gaj, which is some kilometres before Kacuni; is that correct? Could you hear me? Can you hear me, Mr. Kristo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Kristo?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So let us move on. When you left Kiseljak and headed for Busovaca, you dropped by a pub called Jelenov Gaj which is a few kilometres before Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the owner of the place warned you that it would be better for you to head for Busovaca as quickly without delay because there was some gunfire that could be heard from Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And he told you on the same occasion that before you, a military policeman, Ivica Petrovic, had headed in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You knew Ivica Petrovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you followed the advice of the publican and decided it would be better to have some company. So you hurried on your way in order to catch up with Ivica Petrovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you caught up with Ivica Petrovic's vehicle only after you entered Kacuni, somewhere near the crossroads where the road then branches off to the silo which is not far from the mosque.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Ivica Petrovic's vehicle was already stopped in the street when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I object to any further leading of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when your vehicle stopped behind Ivica Petrovic's vehicle, what happened then? Did anyone come up to you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you came to a stop behind Ivica Petrovic's vehicle, did anyone come to your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, at that point, when we caught up with Ivica Petrovic's vehicle, we were surrounded by soldiers of the BH army. They surrounded us from both sides of our vehicle and forced us out. We had to leave the vehicle with the engine switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, those soldiers that were around in that area, were they armed and did you spot what kind of weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. They were armed 100 per cent with automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles and hand-held launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Were some of the rifles also equipped with anti-personnel mines?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So, at some point, you were forced to get off the car?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, they ordered us to get off the car. They ordered me and the driver, Igor Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you -- were you and Igor Bogdanovic wearing civilian clothes or some other clothing?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: We were both wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And what about Ivica Petrovic, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Ivica Petrovic was ahead of us. He was standing by his jeep of the military police, and he was in the military police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, when you left the car, what did those soldiers order you to move in, what direction?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: When we got off the car, they told us to put our hands up and we did so. And they drove us in front -- to move to front of them. They had their rifles aimed at our backs so that we moved under their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In what direction did they tell you to move, or rather, force you to move?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, we moved towards Kacuni, or rather, they took us towards the silo where the BH army was, and their prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just to explain to the Court, they forced you to get off the main road and take a side road in the direction of the silo.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And so you started in that direction. What did you see as you walked down that road towards the silo?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: When we started in front -- ahead of those armed soldiers of the BH army, I cast a look and there were about 10 or 15 vehicles of the then UNPROFOR which were turned heading from Busovaca towards Kiseljak. Some of the vehicles had been diverted towards the silo and other vehicles stayed on the main road from Busovaca to Kiseljak and were stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you observed these vehicles, did you think that you were going to be in a better situation now?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I thought that there would be no problems. I thought that they would be solving the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. What happened in the meantime? Did anybody arrive?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: While we were walking in front of the ABiH soldiers in the direction of their silo, where ABiH soldiers were stationed, and I guess where the prison was, from the direction of Busovaca an armoured vehicle arrived, an HVO vehicle. This was a makeshift armoured vehicle, and it went by the UNPROFOR vehicles which were parked on the road. Even while we were walking with our hands up, under orders of ABiH soldiers, the vehicle approached us, and then the soldiers who were taking us in the direction of silo scattered to the left and right, and they took cover on the side of the road and opened fire on the HVO patrol vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, was this a real armoured vehicle or was it just a truck which had some plates mounted on it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It was an improvised or makeshift vehicle that only had armoured plates put on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said that the soldiers took cover and opened fire on the vehicle. Did they open fire out of small arms or also the heavy weapons? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English Transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, they opened fire on the HVO vehicle, which arrived from the direction Busovaca, out of all the weapons they had on them. I was still on that road with my hands up, and in that moment I saw that from a house -- I saw some red dust coming from this house, that the roof tiles were breaking up and falling. That means that somebody had fired a rocket-propelled grenade at the vehicle but had missed it and hit the roof of this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can move right on to paragraph 14 in your outline. What happened at that time? Did you see what happened to Ivica Petrovic and Igor Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: While I still held my hands up, I saw Ivica Petrovic. At that point, we had parted a little bit, one to the left, one to the right, when the shooting had started. I turned around and I saw Ivica Petrovic who had been hit, and unfortunately he died. I was petrified with fear. And I also saw Igor Bogdanovic as he was trying to cross the road and enter our jeep. However, he was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a semiautomatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to introduce -- to tender several exhibits. We do not need to show it to the witness, but this is death certificates of these two individuals, Ivica Petrovic and Igor Bogdanovic. Also, page 225 of Colonel Stewart's book "Broken Lives," which describes the death of the two individuals at the location which has just been described by the witness. Perhaps we can be given the numbers for the exhibits and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The death certificate of Igor Bogdanovic shall be Defence Exhibit D299/1. The death certificate of Ivica Petrovic shall be Defence Exhibit D300/1. The extract from the book "Broken Lives" shall be Defence Exhibit 301/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, I was about to tell you that the reason for our waiting was of technical nature, because we need to have the exhibits properly registered. So let us conclude about this incident. You were an eyewitness of the deaths of Ivica Petrovic and Igor Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can move through the rest of the outline swiftly. While you were observing what was going on, did you also observe a vehicle which was trying to manoeuvre its way around to turn facing Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. One of the vehicles, one of the UNPROFOR jeeps, was manoeuvreing in the road, moving left and right, trying to turn around in the direction of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you try to use the opportunity to leave this place?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw that this vehicle was turning around, I ran over to it, to this UNPROFOR vehicle. I grabbed the right-hand side. I climbed on it and I grabbed the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you open -- did you say something to the soldiers who were there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There were four soldiers in the vehicle. They were all armed with rifles. They turned to me. I quickly tried to tell them, in German, that I will pose no problem, that I was a civilian, and that I needed to be taken out of this situation, to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So in other words, you asked them to help you, as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So did they help you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: While I was explaining this, that was about ten metres [as interpreted], a soldier who was sitting in the passenger's seat grabbed me by my hands and kicked me off the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you were thrown off the vehicle, but you had moved away from the spot where Ivica Petrovic and Igor Bogdanovic were killed?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And following that, if I follow your outline, you tried to hide.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Still not knowing what was going on, I -- this jeep was moving slowly, so I ran behind it and I ran in the direction of Kacuni and tried to hide in a house, but it was locked. Then I went around it. I saw a shed, and that's where I hid at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Were you able to flee in the direction of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. I could not flee, because I observed soldiers and civilians in the centre of Kacuni and I heard the sounds of unloading of a truck. They were unloading timber, big logs, with which they barricaded the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just to clarify, from the mosque in Kacuni, in order to get to Busovaca, to cross the bridge --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, cross the bridge. And on that location, this is where the truck was unloading the logs, and you could not cross it, either on foot or in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can just move quickly through the paragraph 18. It was wintertime and you were dressed very lightly because you had left your jacket in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. We had left our jackets in the back seat of the vehicle, and we only had light shoes and light tops on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: While you were freezing in that shed for several hours, did you observe that the ABiH soldiers were searching for you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: When I entered the shed, I noticed soldiers and civilians. They were all running towards the road. They were cursing Croats, Ustashas. And they were deploying mines on the road and they were also looking for me. I think that they thought that I had crossed the bridge and fled in that direction, not realising that I was still hiding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Kristo, you've got some paper in front of you which you appear to be reading from. What is the paper, please?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I'm not reading from the paper, and this is probably the paper that you yourself also have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a summary of your evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be better if you put it away and so there's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll proceed swiftly, Mr. Kristo. You spent several hours in the shed and when the dust gathered, you moved on towards the school at Kacuni without realising that the soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Because you were not able to hide there, you moved on. In which direction did you go?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I spent two or three hours in the shed, but this was already dusk, 5.00, 5.30. I moved on towards the school, the elementary school, without realising that the soldiers were there, actually, the ABiH headquarters. So I crawled up to the school building, then I got up. There is an athletic field by the school and I ran across it and entered a forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You hid in the forest almost two days.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Because I was encircled there. I hid there all night walking very quietly through the forest because I did not know the terrain. I had thought that they had set up barricades. I thought that it would have been easiest for me to go in the direction of Kiseljak through the forest. So that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So as you backtracked towards Kiseljak, you arrived in the village of Gusti Grab?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I walked through the forest all night. When they overheard my footsteps, they would open fire. I would then stop and stay quiet, and this is how I went through the night. And the next morning, I arrived in the village called Gusti Grab.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you arrived there, was there fighting there? That is, the attack, had the village been attacked, and who had attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: At that time, it had still not been attacked. But I saw civilians, women, children, packing their bags and suitcases and preparing to leave that place because they had heard that ABiH soldiers were advancing towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could gunfire be heard in the area?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the night and all day the next day, gunfire could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A group of the civilians were transported by buses to Kiseljak and you went with another group.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, we started out towards Kiseljak on foot using village roads, and the dusk again had fallen and the situation calmed down somewhat. We all took shelter in a house owned by Niko Grubesic, that is, his parents, and waited for the buses to come from Kiseljak to pick up the civilians. We waited there for two or three hours because we arrived at that house around midnight and the buses arrived around 5.00 or 6.00. They loaded up as many civilians as they could; children, elderly. They boarded them and they took them in the direction of Kiseljak. Myself and two or three younger men went back to that restaurant called Jelenov Gaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Niko Grubesic's house is in the part of the village called Oseliste?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Their Honours have already heard this, but Niko Grubesic's parents did not leave, they stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: They stayed behind thinking -- they thought they would join the rest later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you hear what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, they were both killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you were leaving Gusti Grab and moving towards Oseliste through the forest, did you notice anything else; fighting or some houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, there was gunfire, there was smoke probably from houses being -- having been set on fire and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kristo, if I understand you correctly, instead of proceeding to Busovaca, you went back to Kiseljak. How many days did you stay in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Because I couldn't go to Busovaca, I returned to Kiseljak and I spent there 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Were the jeep and your valuables, money, ever returned to you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. We tried, but without success.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the last point that I need to ask you about. You are aware that a witness in this matter, I think it was Witness AE, he said that on January 24, which is what you refer -- that only one person was killed, while the second Croat mentioned by this witness allegedly was escorted by the ABiH soldiers in the direction of Busovaca. Is that true what he said?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, it is not true. What is true is that two people were killed, the military policeman, Ivica Petrovic, and the gentleman who was with me in the vehicle, Mr. Igor Bogdanovic. And by sheer luck, I was able to save myself and I survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kristo. I have no further questions. I assume that the Prosecution may have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, I have some questions to ask you for the Prosecution. The cafe that you own in Busovaca, is that the Cafe Bos?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, it's the Cafe Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a cafe that was particularly resorted to by the members of the HVO in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There was no conflict until then and there were no HVO soldiers there, but when the conflict started, they were in the -- in this cafe but I was in Kiseljak, I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You stayed in Kiseljak until when?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I stayed there 17 days. I know that it was exactly 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were back in Busovaca in February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You stayed there throughout the war, is that right, in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the cafe?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, even though it was not working after that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. You gave up the cafe and went to live in Croatia when?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I did not give up the cafe, and I did not move to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You now -- you still live in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've had to travel from Busovaca all the way to Zagreb today or yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in Zagreb two days ago, two days ago, day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just give me one minute, sorry. Have you been in Busovaca then continuously? I'm sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no, it was my mistake. On the 24th of January of 1993, you say you went to buy a jeep. So first you went to Kiseljak, you had to pass that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I went to Kiseljak -- I apologise. I went, but I did not go in a jeep. I went in a passenger vehicle with a friend and I went to get the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that. But first of all, you had to pass the Kacuni checkpoint; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: At that time, there were no checkpoints on the road because had there been any, I wouldn't have gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that there was no checkpoint and no sign of a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, at that time there were no checkpoints. The movement was free from Kiseljak to Konjic, Zenica, anywhere. At least personally, I went there and there were no checkpoints at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was this a road you had been using regularly at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you been on the road, say, the previous day, the 23rd, or the day before that, the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Not a day or two, but perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any previous problem with the same position at Kacuni with there being a checkpoint there? Were you aware of any previous problem?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. There were no checkpoints. And had there been any problems, I probably would not have gone with money on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But Mr. Kristo, four days before all this happened on the 24th, four days earlier, all Muslim businesses in Busovaca had been blown up. You don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. How do you mean, Muslim companies or businesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, shops and cafes and businesses in Busovaca were blown up four days earlier.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't recall that. I don't think there was any of that, because everything was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you in your cafe over the preceding three or four days?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I was there around the clock, because that was my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a murder as well. Do you remember the murder, anything about a murder that happened about four days before, a man called Mirsad Delija?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the 24th of January. You passed the exact place where the checkpoint was subsequently to be, and there was no sign of a checkpoint; there were no barriers, no vehicles, nothing. Is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English Transcripts. the position?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. There was nothing. The road was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what time of the morning do you think it was that you passed on your way for Kiseljak? Half past 8.00? 8.00?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Between 8.00 and 9.00. Around 9.00. I'm not quite sure, but I think it must have been between 8.00 and 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You then went off and bought the jeep, and you paid for that in cash, did you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, before I move on, did you take no part at any stage in the fighting or in the organisation of affairs in Busovaca throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you the only Srecko Kristo in Busovaca, or was there another one?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There are several of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is one of those a military policeman, one of the other ones of the same name?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I do not know him myself. I think he's somewhere from Lasva -- rather, Dusina, where another massacre happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've given an account of coming back, but when you came back, of course, you have to be in three cars all together, don't you: your friend's car, your jeep, and then, by the time you joined up with Petrovic, Petrovic's vehicle. So is it three vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. The friend who had taken us to Kiseljak had gone back, and I and Mr. -- or rather late Igor Bogdanovic, we had gone in his vehicle to get the jeep in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who was this other friend, then? What was the name of this friend who took you all the way there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I think his name was Marko Vuleta. Marko Vuleta and Franjo Drazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you heard of what was the problem ahead at the checkpoint, you joined up with or you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, I'll repeat what I was asking you just before we lost transmission. When you heard of what the problem ahead of you at the checkpoint was, you joined up effectively with Ivica Petrovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: On my way back from Konjic to Kiseljak, and from Kiseljak towards Busovaca, we stopped by the Jelenov Gaj cafe, and there we heard from the owner that something was afoot in Kacuni and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me save you some time. I understand what your account is on that. I'm leaping ahead of you to the place where you say that you joined up with Petrovic, or you caught up with Petrovic. Now, by the time Petrovic got to the checkpoint, had you already caught him up or was he there ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There was no checkpoint, but armed and masked soldiers had stopped Ivica Petrovic's jeep and we had just caught up with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, is it possible that Petrovic had already fired some shots before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. No, he did not, because when we made it where it was, he was disarmed. He had been disarmed. His pistol and his belt were lying down on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, therefore, he may have fired some shots before you ever arrived.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, no, he couldn't have, because we saw him. We were driving behind him, perhaps a kilometre or so. He was stopped by masked and armed soldiers on the road, which was open for traffic and free.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've made reference to UNPROFOR vehicle or vehicles. Was there already an UNPROFOR vehicle at this point in the road at the time that you arrived? Indeed, was it trying to get through?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: When I came up, or rather when we were stopped by those armed troops, UNPROFOR vehicles, the then-UNPROFOR vehicles, some ten or fifteen of them -- I don't know exactly -- were then diverted towards the silo, as you look from Busovaca, and other vehicles were along one of the lanes on the road. But some of them were diverted towards the silo, and that came as a surprise to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What nationality of UNPROFOR do you say it was that was involved here?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know, but I do know that it was UNPROFOR, and one more or less knows who was there in January 1993. Whether they were coming from Busovaca, whether they were just passing by or coming up, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many vehicles all together were there for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I couldn't really say, because it was all happening so fast, but I should say around ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What colour were these vehicles painted? Camouflage colour?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What colour, then?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: White, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just disposing of the UNPROFOR vehicles, you're saying that in due course one of them simply threw you off his vehicle, effectively, when you were turning to him for help. Can you help us at all with the nationality of that person to whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you what state he came from, but in all that fracas and fear, I gripped and took hold of the jeep which was manoeuvreing to go back to Busovaca. And I addressed those soldiers in German, as much as I knew it, to give me a lift to Busovaca because they had already turned and headed for Busovaca. But probably afraid that the troops which had -- who had stopped there and were seizing vehicles might, when firing at me hit, them. That must have been the reason why they simply threw me out of their vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And after your return to Busovaca to dispose of this, you made no complaint to UNPROFOR at all through local officials or on your own account about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, no, I spent 17 days in Kiseljak and by that time, barricades had risen all around so that I came with a Croat and a Muslim through Visoko, Zenica, that is Kakanj, Zenica, to Vitez, and then I returned home in Busovaca. And by that time, it was practically the state of war but it wasn't that, it was saving our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in any event, at the checkpoint itself, a significant number of UNPROFOR vehicles were being blocked and diverted from their chosen route by these men at the checkpoint or whatever we described it as.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I must repeat it once again. There weren't barricades, because had there been any, nobody would have taken the road. It was open, free, for all individuals. Those who wanted to travel could travel and did travel. There were no barricades, there were no roadblocks. Even when I came up, there were no roadblocks there. We were simply stopped by armed troops, and we had to come to a stop because they had aimed at us their rocket launchers and rifles, and we could not stop -- we were stopped at an open place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got there, apart from the men on the road, were there other men, apparently ABiH men, in the fields or whatever on either side of the road?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. What do you mean when I came home?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I said "when I came home," then that's my mistake. When you got to the place where --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I did not get home, I went to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got to the place where the men were in the road is what I was asking you about. When you got to the place where the men held you up, were there other men or were there some men in the fields at the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO KRISTO
