utterances.text: In the course of your work as a humanist, were you asked to assist any of the persons, mainly Muslim civilians and some POWs, who were interned there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not asked at all any assistance. The military had their own offices, they had their own prisoners. I was in charge of certificates and Mr. Darinko Tadic was in charge of the refugees. And I think that that covers my answer, or your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic was the man who you said appointed you to the position that you held at the time. Did Mr. Prlic ask for any input from you about the camps in which these persons were detained before he and Mate Granic from Croatia began to disband the camps in September 1993? Were you involved in that process?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many times did you have dealings with Dario Kordic from the first time until today, please, and when was the first time you met him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, sometime in 1992, and as far as number of meetings is concerned, there were a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Z307, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document which will be placed before you, I want to tell you, is phonetically in your language as it is from packet radio or so it says, and there is an English translation provided. This document is dated, excuse me, I'll wait. The document is dated the 10th of December, 1992. I'm sorry for going back in time a little, but I must ask you this, and it is sent from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Busovaca regional staff to the Croat Defence Council presidents of a number of municipalities listed above and is signed by Dario Kordic. Now, at this -- what is asked or what is demanded is that these persons supply the data of persons killed, persons missing, names and ages of children of soldiers killed in action, the severely wounded, those taken prisoner, number of pensioners in the municipality, number of unemployed, number of exiles and refugees, and Kordic directs persons who are responsible for collecting this data to send this information to you. You were a minister, were you not, at that time or you were a head of a department at that time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. In order to be able to compile a sociological picture of what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So Mr. Kordic could direct your functions as well. He's signing here as vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and he is ordering certain things to happen and he's ordering you to do certain things. Are there any other occasions that you can think of where you received such orders initiated by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall a single order by Mr. Kordic reaching me because I was exclusively answerable to Mr. Prlic as the prime minister. I don't see whether this -- I couldn't read the text, whether this was an order to me personally, but I know that in my ministry, that the request went out to all the municipalities to compile these -- this information in order so that we could the picture of what we had on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You made mention of a number of Muslim ministers, and this Court has heard a reasonable amount of testimony about these persons. Are you aware of from where these Muslims came, were they natives of Central Bosnia or do you know anything about their origins? For example, do you know if they were from Posavina?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the Muslim ministers were from, except for those with whom I worked more closely. I know that the minister, Resad Bektic was from Sarajevo, Mr. Munir Jahic was from Tuzla. He was also a professor at the university. Then minister of the interior was from eastern Bosnia. He was a -- in the BH government while I was there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At what point in time were these persons engaged in ministry-level positions, can you tell us from when to when, please?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the democratic elections they were appointed. The government replaced the communist government in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those were my colleagues, and some of them remained in their positions and some did not. I don't know when Mr. Muhamedcengic left. I don't know when Alija Delimustafic left, he went abroad. I don't know about Munir Jahic and so on. I only saw Mr. Resad Bektic who was the minister for economic affairs, he was later in Zagreb. So that's all I can say about all these ministers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have noticed and I must ask you this question, I apologise that it got skipped, I think it was because of the break coming. But when you listed earlier the number of Croats who were part of the BiH government at various points in time, I noticed that you did not list Stjepan Siber, why would that be?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Siber was not in the government in my time, he was neither minister nor deputy minister. He may have had some lower-ranking position in one of the ministries so I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, actually he was the deputy commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you confirm that of the group that you listed, only Jerko Doko did not go over to the HZ HB side; is that a correct assessment of political affiliations?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult to look inside people to -- when -- considering who went where. It also has to do with who was involved to what extent. I had a meeting very recently with Mr. Jerko Doko, he was not involved in affairs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and/or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think it's time to put an end to the cross-examination because this is about the end of the time that had been given to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask the Court's indulgence for a final question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had suggested that the only persons who supported Stjepan Kljuic were the Sarajevo-based HDZ persons. May I ask you, do you know Martin Udovicic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English Transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I shall repeat it. You had indicated in your testimony that the principle base of support for Mr. Kljuic was the Sarajevo HDZ members. My question to you is: Did you know Martin Udovicic? Do you know the man?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. He was the president in old Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right. And are you aware of Mr. Udovicic unflinching support for Stjepan Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of him supporting him that much because he was also saying that he didn't support him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is that based on your reading minutes by Ignac Kostroman? Is your conclusion of his not supporting Kljuic based on the minutes of various HDZ meetings taken by Ignac Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I personally was in a situation when my father was ill and he was in Novi Travnik, and I frequently was in communication with Mr. Martin and he was telling me the opposite of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One last question: Did you ask for any information about Ahmici, about the events of Ahmici when you were in Central Bosnia with Kresimir Zubak and Mr. Zoran Buntic? You, as a former religious person and humanist, did you follow up on anything there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked for no information and I said that I felt for all the people who suffered and I sympathised with their families. And had I had an opportunity, I would have gone there and help out these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, thank you for coming to the -- into the office to make your -- to give your evidence to the Tribunal. You are now free to go. Your evidence being over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not terribly familiar with this set up with the monitors. I have been asked to raise three housekeeping matters, two and then one follow-up on something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you might get on your feet now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We need to request time to deal with an affidavit tomorrow that has come in, and if we could be granted that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Also we'd ask the Defence to provide the summary immediately for Ante Puljic. He is a significant witness, and we anticipate a lot of work tonight on that. And further, during the break, on the matter that I raised about the translation issue of the Zuljevic summary, we've confirmed our concern over inaccuracy with the interpreters, and we will present that in some form. If the court would like it verbally, we can do it, or we can do it in a written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I shall think in a written form if you will, Ms. Somers. Yes, we ought to deal with as many affidavits as we can tomorrow because there have been some in last week and also we must hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, half past nine. 2

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
